brief: Deutsche Bank's Henry Allen argues the market's three dominant bear cases (a Mideast oil shock, an AI slowdown, and European fiscal-spread stress) rarely hit together because they offset: an AI scare lowers bond yields and growth expectations, which cools inflation and eases fiscal strain, making it its own partial hedge. That logic reversed this past week. Oil, AI/credit and OAT-Bund stress had all eased since October (Brent fell to $96.58, the Philly semiconductor index rose over 12% off its November 5 low, credit spreads tightened, the OAT-Bund spread narrowed from 174bps to 156bps), letting the S&P post a weekly gain. But that easing gave central banks room to keep hiking: US core CPI's 3-month annualized pace hit 3.75% in October, Trump ruled out an Iran deal, and markets now price 113bps of total Fed hikes by September 2027 versus 95bps priced before this cycle began. Allen's one exception is oil: a new Hormuz escalation (Iran's closure declaration, a mined tanker, a third US carrier) raises inflation and fiscal stress while squeezing growth, so it alone does not offset. Deutsche's own call favors the hawkish path.
